item.title: Mary Peltola nears an Alaska Senate win as Democrats eye a 56th seat
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Campaign signs on October 30, 2026 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) Democrat Mary Peltola has widened her lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's still-undecided U.S. Senate race, moving within striking distance of an outright victory that would give Democrats their 56th Senate seat following sweeping midterm gains. As of Saturday morning, Peltola had 49.8% of the vote, compared with Sullivan's 46.1%, a margin of more than 10,000 votes. The Associated Press reported 96% of votes counted, with Peltola receiving 138,240 votes to Sullivan's 127,828. The former congresswoman gained nearly 2,000 votes on Sullivan in the latest batch of ballots, strengthening her prospects of clearing the 50% threshold needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice voting tabulation. Peltola's campaign declared victory Friday, insisting the Republican incumbent could no longer overcome her advantage. "There is no mathematical path for Sullivan to win this race," the campaign said in a statement posted on X. "When the remaining votes are counted, Mary will decisively be elected as Alaska’s next United States Senator," the statement read. Campaign manager Cheryl Bruce echoed that confidence in a statement to Newsweek. "As more ballots get counted, it’s clear that Mary’s victory is all but guaranteed, and Alaskans have resoundingly rejected Dan Sullivan’s D.C. self dealing," Bruce said. "Mary won today’s ballot drop by a decisive margin, and remaining votes from Anchorage, Juneau, and rural Alaska will continue to break for Mary, continuing her momentum to the United States Senate. "Alaskans are ready for a senator who fights to lower costs and takes on D.C. corruption, and when every vote is counted, Mary will deliver for Alaska," Bruce said. Sullivan's campaign, however, declined to concede. "We’re still waiting for every ballot to be counted. And we’ll see what happens from there," campaign spokesman Nate Adams told The New York Times on Friday. The race remained uncalled Saturday, with outstanding ballots potentially determining whether Peltola secures an outright majority or must prevail through ranked-choice voting. Under Alaska's system, if no candidate receives more than 50% of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidates are eliminated and their supporters' subsequent preferences redistributed until a winner emerges. Two minor candidates, Republican Gerald Heikes and unaffiliated Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., have collectively captured roughly 4% of the vote. Democrats recruited both candidates in an effort to weaken the incumbent's support, according to The New York Times. The Trump administration previously challenged the election over the presence of another candidate named Sullivan, arguing potential voter confusion, but the lawsuit was dismissed. Alaska has until Nov. 18 to complete its vote count, with ranked-choice tabulation to follow if necessary. A Peltola victory would represent another significant Democratic pickup in a midterm election that has already delivered the party 55 Senate seats, its largest majority since the early Obama administration. Peltola, who campaigned on "fish, family, and freedom," would become the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate and the first Democrat to win an Alaska Senate seat in nearly two decades. Her potential victory would also underscore Republican difficulties in a state President Donald Trump carried by approximately 14 percentage points in 2024, amid voter concerns over high prices, the administration's war in Iran, and tariffs affecting Alaska's economy. In another major Democratic victory in Alaska, former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, has won the state's gubernatorial election, defeating three Republican opponents in a four-way contest, according to Decision Desk HQ. Kreiss-Tomkins will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, becoming Alaska's youngest governor and the first Democrat elected to the office in more than two decades. His victory came after national political organizations poured millions into the contest, with Democrats benefiting from a divided Republican field despite Trump's endorsement of Bernadette Wilson. Meanwhile, Alaska's U.S. House race remains uncalled, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich III leading in a contest expected to proceed to ranked-choice tabulation. © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: U.K. to consider new age of consent law after Russell Brand accuser speaks out
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
British comedian and TV star Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and 6 months on 9 November after being convicted for rape and sexual assaults. Photograph: Brook Mitchell/AFP/Getty Images The government has said it will consider calls to change the age of consent after a woman waived her right to anonymity to publicly claim she was raped by Russell Brand as a 16-year-old schoolgirl. Mia Latter, now 37, alleged she had been orally raped by the jailed comedian when she was a teenager and he was 30 years old. In an interview with the Sunday Times, she called for the introduction of a staggered age of consent – which would make relationships between adults and teenagers aged 16 and 17 illegal. Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, told the newspaper that Latter’s “heart-breaking story” meant a law change deserved consideration. She said: “We need to listen to Mia and other victims like her who have been through these experiences because it’s really important that as lawmakers their experience is at the heart of what we consider. “It clearly would be a massive step to change the age of consent, but it deserves proper consideration and scrutiny. I can absolutely understand why she is calling for it.” Under UK law, adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds. Latter said: “It’s shocking to me time and time again that whenever the news comes up again about him, it’s always in the comments about the relationship with a 16-year-old. “That’s not the most heinous bit. But why is that the thing that everybody collectively gets stuck on? I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.” Latter was referred to under the pseudonym of Alice in previous reporting by the Sunday Times, the Times, and Channel 4’s Dispatches documentary. She was 16 when she first met Brand in Leicester Square, central London, while she was on her way home from a shopping trip. He took her number and later messaged her, asking if she wanted to go for dinner, she said. She told the newspaper that Brand – who was working at MTV at the time – still asked her to meet after she had confessed her age to him. Latter alleges Brand orally raped her towards the end of their three-month relationship. Brand denied all of the allegations made against him by Latter when they were first reported in 2023 by the Times. She spoke to the police after the documentary, but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decided not to include her case in Brand’s trial at Southwark Crown Court. He was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is now serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults. Earlier this week, it was announced that a series of “serious” sex offence allegations against comedian David Walliams are being probed by the Metropolitan police after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”. Walliams denies any wrongdoing. Haigh went on to say that, in light of news that one of Walliams’s accusers was asked to sign a non disclosure agreement (NDA), the government should also look at banning them in cases of alleged sexual assault and harassment. She said: “When we consider the allegations against David Walliams, teenagers who were fans wouldn’t come under the current consultation. “I do think there is a very strong case to look at banning NDAs in all circumstances where they relate to harassment or discrimination, to make sure that no victim, regardless of where it happened or what their relationship was with the perpetrator, should ever be silenced.” It is believed MPs outside Labour may support a bill to change the age of consent laws, with Jess Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson, coming out in favour of reviewing them. Commending Latter for the “extraordinary bravery” it took to waive her anonymity, Brown-Fuller said: “I think we must go further to increase protections for young women and girls, and looking at a staggered age of consent is an important step. “We already have rules that recognise power imbalances in professions: between teachers and students, or barristers and junior colleagues. It’s time for the government to recognise the implicit power imbalance held by older men over teenage girls.” Latter’s decision to come forward was also praised by Bridget Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, who said she “and thousands of others across the country will be in awe of her courage and determination”. She added that it is “up to all of us to send a message to women and girls who experience sexual violence: the shame is not yours. Women like Mia are leading the charge, but we can and must do more to make this a moment of change.” Latter’s allegation was reported to the Met police, who said the investigation into the alleged rape remains ongoing. A Met Police spokesperson said: “Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape. “Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made. “This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence.” The CPS said: “The Crown Prosecution Service will continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible.” This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/uk-government-consider-changing-age-001714446.html

item.title: U.S. is facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Russia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The United States is facilitating direct engagement between Russia and Europe amid a push to secure a peace deal in the war in Ukraine , President Trump's special envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Saturday. Kushner and Steve Witkoff held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this past week as the Trump administration pushes to end the more than 4 ½-year conflict. The meetings came after the first round of U.S.-brokered talks between the two countries since February concluded on Wednesday with an announcement of plans for a new prisoner exchange and further talks, but nothing to suggest a wider peace deal. "Our focus is now on facilitating direct engagement between Moscow and European partners and preparing the agenda for the next round of trilateral talks," Kushner said in a social media post on Saturday. "Several new ideas emerged from these discussions and are now being explored. Some may lead to breakthroughs directly, while others may evolve into new proposals that help bridge the remaining gaps." Zelenskyy, in statements released Saturday, said the U.S. had raised the possibility of a new security framework for Europe, though he warned that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent's borders. "In my view, this can be dangerous," Zelenskyy told reporters Friday, referring to the new security framework. "This should not be the main agenda." His comments were embargoed until Saturday. Zelenskyy said the U.S. had asked for the first time whether Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russia does not control if Kyiv were admitted to NATO. He reiterated that Kyiv would not surrender its territory. He also said he believed Moscow was interested in reopening broader questions about European security rather than focusing exclusively on ending the war. "Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe," he said. "This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations." European leaders have stressed that decisions about the continent's security must be made by Europeans themselves, warning against allowing Russia to dictate the terms of a new security order or negotiate NATO's future. Ukraine is discussing a comprehensive security package with its partners that could include specific guarantees from NATO and the European Union, a strong Ukrainian military and financial support for a specified period, he said. It would also include a recovery plan, he said. "If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: Do we accept it or not?" Zelenskyy said. He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognizing occupied territories as Russian. Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country's constitution. "If Putin expects Ukraine's neutrality to be enshrined, that's not going to happen," he said. "We're not in NATO right now anyway." Kushner said Saturday that a lasting peace in Ukraine requires security guarantees for Kyiv and "detailed, actionable postwar security arrangements that reduce the risk of another war." "NATO will remain a critical pillar of European security, enhanced by stronger mechanisms for military, communication, deconfliction, and reciprocal de-escalation, with practical ways to address disputes before they become crises," he added. "This is why we are working to bring our European partners directly into these discussions. Any final agreement must be agreed to by the relevant parties, and President Trump will only support arrangements that strengthen Ukraine's and Europe's security and make future conflict less likely." Zelenskyy warned that broader discussions about Europe's security could allow Putin to seek changes to NATO's military presence, including the withdrawal of American troops. He said Putin had raised similar ideas with then-President Joe Biden in 2021, seeking a redistribution of power in Europe and the world. "I think Putin will bring up Finland and Sweden. I'm sure he will raise the issue of Hungary and the presence of American troops in the Baltic countries," Zelenskyy said. He said any changes to Europe's security arrangements must be decided by European NATO members only after the war ends. "The sequence should be as follows: a ceasefire, an end to the war in Ukraine, and security guarantees for Ukraine," he said. "There can be no security guarantees in Europe, or for Europe, without Ukraine." Mr. Trump is set to meet with Putin next week as part of a trilateral summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. He is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, officials said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/us-europe-russia-engagement-ukraine-war/

item.title: U.S. floated idea of Ukraine surrendering territory for NATO membership, Zelensky says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Olena Harmash KYIV, Nov 14 (Reuters) - US negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine's potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, following the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi. This is the first time ‌the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelenskiy said in remarks to reporters released by his office ‌on Saturday. "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" he said. "That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's signals, ​and this is an extremely difficult conversation." Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia's full-blown invasion in 2022. Zelenskiy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum. 'THIS WAR MUST BE ENDED FIRST' Echoing comments made by European leaders at a ‌summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskiy dismissed Russia's call ⁠for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine. "We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent ⁠overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first," he said. US President Donald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said on Saturday that the two sides had set out "maximalist positions" in the talks this week, but in private discussions both "understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war." "Serious and constructive work continues among those of ​us ​committed to finding solutions," Kushner said in a social media post. Zelenskiy also dismissed Putin's suggestion for ​a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, a hotly contested city in ‌Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, saying it reflected Moscow's inability to take the city by force. Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added. "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way," he said. Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other frontline settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Zelenskiy said. Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war. LARGE PRISONER EXCHANGE AGREED The two days of US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough, though the sides agreed to ‌a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Zelenskiy said. The final numbers for ​the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added. Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff had pledged ​to raise an energy ceasefire with Putin at a meeting in Moscow on ​Thursday, Zelenskiy said, but there was no news of any progress after their talks. "Putin personally does not support a ceasefire," he said. Zelenskiy ‌met Witkoff and Kushner on Thursday in Ireland after their talks ​in Moscow. He said the US negotiators had ​told him that all sides had agreed for Europe to have a seat at the negotiating table in forthcoming peace talks. In Abu Dhabi, delegates from Europe — which is now Ukraine's largest financial and military backer — had talks with US and Ukrainian officials but did not sit at the table with Russia. At ​the summit in Ireland, EU leaders agreed that Europe's team ‌for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers — non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland — as well as EU ​officials. Kushner said the US focus was now on "facilitating direct engagement between Moscow and European partners and preparing the agenda for the next round of ​trilateral talks." (Reporting by Olena Harmash; Editing by Daniel Flynn, Gareth Jones and Sanjeev Miglani) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/us-floated-idea-ukraine-ceding-122531169.html

item.title: Investigators seek why tanker 'lost control' as it hit cruise ship in New Orleans
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Passengers of a river cruise boat in New Orleans had to be pulled from the Mississippi river on Friday after a tanker collided with the paddlewheeler as it sat in dock, causing it to capsize. Those aboard desperately gripped the railings of the American Heritage as it started taking on water and tipping over, sparking a major emergency response. In what Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry hailed as a “miracle on the Mississippi,” all 197 passengers made it to safety. “There had to be some kind of divine, godly intervention for this outcome,” Mayor Helena Moreno said Saturday. Hours after the collision, the Port of New Orleans sued to ensure the seizure of the tanker, Atlantic Asphalt, which the lawsuit said is owned and managed by a Liberia-based shipping company. The lawsuit, which also named Thome Ship Management in Singapore, said the tanker caused more than $1 million in damage to a New Orleans terminal. The docked riverboat was struck “as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness” of the tanker, Nave Shipping and Thome, according to the suit. CNN has reached out to Thome for comment and is attempting to contact the tanker’s owner. Moreno said 32 people were taken to hospitals with noncritical injuries, while others were treated at the scene for “bumps and bruises.” On Saturday, city officials said eight remained in hospitals – two in serious condition, the others stable. The Atlantic Asphalt appeared to have “lost control,” according to US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham, who added that the “exact reason why” it may have lost steering capabilities remained unknown. “I do not have any indication that this is terrorism-related,” Burnham added. Investigators are on scene collecting evidence and plan to begin interviewing crew members in the coming days, National Transportation Safety Board officials said in a Saturday afternoon news briefing. The American Heritage river cruise boat is seen on its side after being struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker ship, top center, in the Mississippi River in New Orleans, on Friday, November 13. - Gerald Herbert/AP Screams for help In dramatic video from the scene, a distinct metallic screech can be heard as the vessels collide. At least a dozen people wearing life vests can later be seen being pulled from the water, while other passengers clamber over the railings of the boat, lying on its side in the Mississippi. About 80 people were evacuated from the boat before it capsized, said New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll. Numerous vessels immediately rushed to the scene to rescue passengers from the river. “It was all hands on deck,” the mayor said. “First responders, other boats and vessels that were in proximity all raced to do what they could to help,” Moreno told reporters. Joe Knab, a passenger visiting New Orleans from Wichita, told CNN affiliate WDSU the hulking tanker was blasting its horn as it floated toward the riverboat. Moments later, he was in the water without a life jacket, clutching a pillow to stay afloat and a woman holding onto his feet. “It was a little scary there at the time when I think I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath,” he said, adding he was in the water for 15 to 20 minutes. Knab wore a T-shirt from a Hilton hotel where passengers stayed Friday night. His other shirts and belongings were “at the bottom of the river,” he said. “My phone still works. That’s amazing. I got my wallet,” he said. His roommate on the boat, however, lost everything. Truck driver Blas Armas, who recorded on his phone as panicked passengers tried to swim from the stricken boat, said many elderly people in the river screamed, “Help, help.” “The most terrifying thing was an old lady (who had) only her head out of the water,” Armas told CNN late Friday. “She was wearing a vest, but it wasn’t around her neck,” he said, adding that she was trying to swim with one hand as she clung to what looked like a piece of floating furniture. The woman was eventually pulled to safety. He also recalled seeing an elderly man bleeding from his forehead. “People were scared,” he said. Brian Clesi, captain of the New Orleans riverboat Creole Queen, was on his way to work Friday when he received a phone call: A ship had lost steering about a quarter mile away. Clesi and Ellis “Jimmy” Kimball later launched the riverboat’s bow-mounted rescue boat and made their way to the crash site, where rescuers were already plucking people from the river. Clesi, 53, told CNN he and his partner pulled nine people out of the water and took them to other vessels for triage or to first responders on the riverbank. They brought one man with head trauma to a fireboat. “About three people we responded to, including one harbor police officer, were wearing life jackets. But the rest that we pulled out were not. So, it was imperative to get them to safety as soon as possible,” Clesi said. “I’m just glad we were there to get them out,” he said. “The ones that didn’t have a life jacket on were holding on for dear life.” Many of the people in the water were elderly and appeared to be in shock, Clesi said. “We train for this. We do man overboard drills, rescue drills, fire drills,” Clesi said. “Everybody in this harbor works together as a team. If somebody is in need, everybody’s coming. So, it wasn’t just us. We played a very small part in the grand scheme of things.” Moreno, the mayor, said passengers began disembarking after the cruise ship was first hit, but it then began to sink and eventually “toppled over and flipped.” New Orleans firefighters immediately responded to the collision and used ladders over the dock to try to rescue people, Moreno said. Other ships on the Mississippi River also responded to help get people out of the water, she added. American Cruise Lines, the owner of the riverboat American Heritage, confirmed its boat was involved in the incident and said it worked with local authorities to evacuate everyone from the vessel. Thome, the ship management company responsible for implementing the International Safety Management code on the boat, said in a statement that the Atlantic Asphalt tanker was built in 2017 and registered in the Marshall Islands. “We deeply regret the impact of this incident and extend our sincere concern and heartfelt sympathies to those injured. Our thoughts remain with the passengers of the AMERICAN HERITAGE following their harrowing experience as we work diligently to assess and investigate the incident,” the company said, adding that it was “fully complying with the local authorities.” The American Heritage was built in 2015 and has capacity for 150 guests, according to the operator . The cruise line, which offers river cruises across the US, hosts several cruises that port in New Orleans. The person driving the tanker was a river pilot, said Burnham, the Coast Guard captain. This image taken from a video shows people being helped out of the water after a tanker crashed into a river cruise in New Orleans, on Friday, November 13 - Devon Flanagan/AP Some passengers abandoned personal items on the sinking ship, Moreno said, and are now staying at local hotels. The city is working with partners, including the American Red Cross, to ensure all passengers have access to accommodation, transportation and necessary prescription medications. Two harbor police officers that had been hospitalized were released Friday evening, the Port of New Orleans said in an update. Landry, the governor, praised all of the agencies involved, saying their constant partnership prepared them for this type of situation. “It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi,” he said. “When you think about the population that was on that cruise ship, and the ability for us to get them off, get them out of the water.” “The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond, right? I mean, there were challenges out there,” he added. President Donald Trump, who offered the state support, also praised first responders, saying in a social media post, “All of Law Enforcement and First Responders were fantastic!” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that “by the grace of God, we have not lost one soul” during the collision and subsequent rescue. unknown content item - Following the rescue mission, the US Coast Guard has reopened the main channel to limited traffic after it was shut down immediately following the collision, Burnham said. It could take weeks to remove the American Heritage from the river, the mayor said. Before the riverboat is moved, Burnham said, its 16,000 gallons of fuel need to be removed. In the initial phase of the NTSB investigation, officials recovered the tanker’s voyage data recorder, according to John DeLeeuw, an NTSB board member. The device is similar to a flight data recorder on airplanes, and it tracks information including the ship’s maneuvers, course and audio from the bridge, Andrew Ehlers, deputy director of marine safety at NTSB, told reporters Saturday afternoon. Investigators will be at the collision scene for about a week, DeLeeuw said. Officials will interview crew members and others involved, and they will work to collect any remaining evidence on scene, including from the river boat that is partially submerged in about 25 feet of water. The NTSB will issue its preliminary report in about a month, followed by a final report released between 18 and 24 months later, DeLeeuw said. Landry said there “is an active investigation” into the collision. “We want to make sure that this investigation is thorough, we understand exactly what happened, so that we can triage those problems and ensure that the Mississippi River remains a very safe place,” he said. This story has been updated with additional information. CNN’s Aaron Cooper, Sarah Dewberry, Taylor Galgano, Jason Morris, Jada Furlow and Shawn Nottingham contributed to this report For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/13/us/new-orleans-tanker-crash

item.title: Biggest waves in a decade pound California beaches and flood streets
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Chris Aceves, center, with the help of friends Natalie Nunez and David Lechuga, carries a sandbag to protect his Pacifica home from flooding caused by huge waves Saturday. From left: Natalie Nunez, Chris Aceves and David Lechuga try to protect Aceves' home from flooding caused by huge waves Saturdasy in Pacifica. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) The Bay Area's biggest waves in more than a decade slammed the California coast Saturday, flooding streets, endangering homes and threatening to engulf anyone who got too close. The waves attracted onlookers from the North Bay to Santa Cruz County, dousing many with cold water as they ran to higher ground. Related: California could see another round of mammoth waves within days Pacifica was hit especially hard, with large waves consistently crashing over its seawall and flooding city streets. Every 30 minutes or so, a wave that appeared to be double the size of the previous one pushed water hundreds of feet inland. Onlookers were soaked by the towers of water, sometimes knocking people off their feet and sending them scrambling in many directions. Rocks, kelp and other debris surrounded the famous Taco Bell Cantina, and nearly a foot of floodwater along Highway 1 prevented cars from entering the parking lot. A high surf warning was in effect until Sunday morning for "life-threatening" waves of 25 to 35 feet, potentially 50 to 60 feet at steep shorelines such as Mavericks in Half Moon Bay, the National Weather Service said. As of 9 a.m. Saturday, significant wave heights - the average of the highest third of waves - were measured up to 31 feet at a buoy offshore Point Reyes, the second largest in three decades of records. Only in December 2015 were waves bigger, by less than a foot. Maximum waves are often 1.8 times bigger than the significant wave height. Waves probably surpassed 50 feet at many offshore buoys, though there are limited official measurements along the immediate coast. "Typically, the largest waves arrive in December and January, and only one time in the 27-year record of the Point Reyes buoy have forecast wave heights been this large in November," the Scripps Institution of Oceanography said in a social media post. Homeowners and renters scramble as massive waves flood garages, basements and cars in Pacifica during one of California's largest wave events in decades. 🎥: Anthony Edwards Read more >> https://t.co/p4lpCNWRE2 https://t.co/0kcbjLv0Vd - San Francisco Chronicle (@sfchronicle) November 14, 2026 Another large swell was expected late Sunday into Monday, with rough seas continuing through the week as more storms spin off the California coast. Erin Shea, a renter at the end of Elder Lane in Pacifica, said floodwater damaged personal belongings in her garage. Adam Drake watches as flooding from high waves inundates a street outside his Pacifica home Saturday. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) Adam Drake, a beachfront homeowner farther up Elder Lane, said the scenes of the waves were "unprecedented," with only 2023 bringing more furious flooding. Recently installed pumps were not working to drain floodwater at the end of the road. Marc Ramos, who surfs at Rockaway Beach in Pacifica at least twice a week, said Saturday's rip currents arrived early in the season and made surfing impossible. "This is just the beginning of the surf season," Ramos said as he checked out the scene. "I've seen it like this, but in mid-January. This is kind of odd. We haven't even hit Thanksgiving yet." Ramos said anyone getting too close to the waves could be swept out to sea pretty quickly. "Don't go out," he said. "Definitely don't go out." Near the Pacifica Pier, a constant stream of onlookers flocked to the waterfront on foot despite closures on adjacent streets due to safety concerns. Several spectators, including a mother carrying a toddler, were caught in a sneaker wave and knocked down in the parking lot in front of the Pacifica City Council Chambers. The mother and toddler were able to get up with the help of bystanders who immediately jumped in to assist. About 50 people stood along San Francisco's Ocean Beach near Sunset Dunes park watching the waves late Saturday morning. The tide went all the way to the dune in front of the parking lot. Among the onlookers was Emir Molina, who has been fishing on Ocean Beach since he moved to San Francisco 26 years ago. The waves were far too big for him to fish Saturday, he said. Molina said the waves were the biggest he's seen in all those years. November is later than he usually sees vicious waves along the coast of San Francisco, he said. They usually come in October, and they don't go nearly as far out. "I have a ton of respect for the ocean," he said. "A ton of respect." Waves crash onto the Pacifica coast Saturday. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) In Marin County, Richard Delameter came to Point Reyes Beach from Novato to watch the waves. "Why am I here? Because nature, when she is furious, is completely dramatic. I like the drama of watching the earth when she's angry," he said. Delameter said he had been coming to Point Reyes since 1967. Earlier Saturday, he was picking up debris from the beach "but the ranger told me to get my ass up to higher ground." With high tide coming at 12:45 p.m., Delameter said "another hour and I can get back to college football." Onlookers check out the waves Saturday at Point Reyes Beach. (J.K. Dineen/S.F. Chronicle) While the waves were dramatic, U.S. Park Service volunteer Susan Aaron said the sunshine and relatively light breeze were having a moderating effect. "If the wind was blowing another 20 miles per hour, the waves would be right up to the base of the dunes," she said. Aaron said she is expecting the winter to bring extensive damage to the California coast. "The coastal communities are in real trouble. People are unaware of the power of nature." Redwood City resident Edward Dorville went to Stinson Beach, but the surf there was not too impressive so he drove to Point Reyes. "Here the surf is more irregular so I thought there would be more impact. Humbling is the word," he said. "It's a reminder." Workers watch tidal water in Soquel Creek during high surf Saturday in Capitola (Santa Cruz County). (Noah Berger/For the S.F. Chronicle) The Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office issued a weekend evacuation warning for low-lying coastal areas due to significant wave activity and hazardous surf conditions. "Large waves have the potential to reach coastal homes and properties, causing dangerous flooding and making access to affected areas difficult or unsafe," the sheriff's office said. The National Weather Service warned spectators to keep a safe distance from the waves all along the California coast. Onlookers scramble as a wave breaks at Steamer Lane in Santa Cruz on Saturday. (Noah Berger/For the S.F. Chronicle) "Dangerously large breaking waves can overpower swimmers, pulling people into the sea from beaches, jetties, and rocks resulting in significant physical injury and increasing the risk of drowning," the weather service said. "Waves can sweep across the shoreline without warning." Huge waves are a hallmark of El Niño , and experts say repeated rounds of waves this winter could cause billions of dollars in damage along the California coast, especially if they hit during high tides. "El Niño-driven changes in tropical weather patterns are shifting storm paths across the North Pacific, bringing stronger storms and bigger waves to the California coast," Scripps said in its social media post. "During El Niño, storms also tend to track farther south, forming closer to California and increasing wave activity along the coast." Waves break at the Walton Lighthouse in Santa Cruz on Saturday. (Noah Berger/For the S.F. Chronicle) These large waves generate tremendous energy. The relationship between wave heights and energy is a squared relation, meaning a 40-foot wave slams into the coast with four times as much energy as a 20-foot wave. Along the California coast, wave power is 32% stronger during strong El Niños than a typical year. Wave-producing storms are becoming larger with climate change, and rising sea levels are contributing to more coastal damage, previous research found. item.title: Mike Johnson says GOP losses drove his decision to step away from House leadership
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Mike Johnson said he decided to leave his leadership role ‘pretty quickly after election night’. Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty Images In his first interview since the midterm elections , the US House speaker, Mike Johnson , said that the Republican party’s crushing losses during the 3 November elections prompted his decision to step away from party leadership. “Leaders have to take responsibility when things go wrong,” Johnson said on Fox News on Saturday. The Republican leader, who informed aides on 4 November that he would not seek re-election for House leadership, said on Saturday that he reached the decision “pretty quickly after election night”. “We worked around the clock, left it all on the field to win. We had to defy history, as you and I both know, it’s only happened twice in 90 years, but we did everything that we could to make that happen,” Johnson said. “But, you know, this was the a year where history was not defied … Related: Progressive versus moderate? Democrats deny party rift as they head into new Congress “We don’t like the results,” he said. “But, real leadership, I’ve always believed, you lead from the front, and leaders have to take responsibility when things go wrong whether it’s individually deserved or not, that’s part of it … “I’m going to remain in this fight, but from a role different than as minority leader in the next Congress,” he added. Johnson’s decision came after Republicans suffered historic losses in this year’s midterm elections, with Democrats flipping key seats in Republican strongholds, including Texas, to seize control of both the Senate and House . It stood in sharp contrast to the reaction of Donald Trump, who has deflected all responsibility for the devastating losses suffered by his party, including defeats for at least 10 Republican Senate candidates in states where he held rallies in the closing weeks of the campaign. That number could rise to 11, should Alaska’s incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, be defeated. As it stands, come 3 January, Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate, and Republicans will have 44. In the House, Democrats will have at least 256 seats, while Republicans will have at least 169. Each party leads in four of the eight House races where votes are still being counted , and the final two seats will be determined in runoff elections next month in Louisiana. The Senate race in Alaska has not yet been called. On Tuesday, House Republicans elected the congressman Jim Jordan, of Ohio, to replace Johnson next year, when Republicans will be the minority party in both chambers of Congress. Senate Republicans, meanwhile, re-elected the senator John Thune, of South Dakota, to continue as their leader. Democrats have not yet voted on who will lead their party in the House and Senate when the new Congress convenes in January. The representative Hakeem Jeffries, of New York, currently serves as House minority leader for the Democrats, and is expected to become the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, while the senator Chuck Schumer, also of New York, currently leads Senate Democrats. However, the contest for Senate leadership has intensified in recent days, after Chris Van Hollen , of Maryland, announced a challenge to Schumer for the position. “In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority leader.” Bernie Sanders, the progressive senator from Vermont, said this week that he would not support Schumer’s bid to serve as the Democratic leader in the Senate, saying that “the time is now for change”. Sanders then endorsed Van Hollen and outlined the stakes of that contest in a Guardian opinion article . Senate Democrats are scheduled to hold a closed-door vote on 1 December . Currently, Jeffries does not face a challenger, but he has faced resistance from some members of his party, including from several Democrats elected earlier this month. item.title: A botched router upgrade grounded flights nationwide. Now questions are mounting.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By David Shepardson WASHINGTON, Nov 14 (Reuters) - US air travel is not expected to return to normal schedules until late on Sunday, the head of the FAA said, as the aviation system gradually recovers from a nationwide flight shutdown that officials blamed on routine maintenance gone awry. As of 9:35 p.m. ET (0235 GMT), airlines on Saturday had ‌canceled more than 6,400 US flights and delayed more than 8,000, according to FlightAware, an aviation website. That followed about 9,200 flights canceled and 7,500 delayed on Friday after ‌the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop because of disruptions to air traffic communications. FlightAware said 875 flights scheduled for Sunday were already canceled. Federal Aviation Administration head Bryan Bedford said on Saturday that he expected airline operations to largely return to ​normal by late Sunday. He also apologized for the disruption, adding that the system remains stable. The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours. It was the longest nationwide halt to air travel since the attacks of September 11, 2001, and one of the single worst US travel days ever. The issue prompted the White House to convene an emergency meeting in the Situation Room on Friday and federal agencies to scramble to determine if it was a cyberattack. But the problem was traced to FAA contractor L3Harris' installation of at least one new router at a remote ‌facility, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday. "We're working to determine ⁠whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said at a press conference. The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, a union representing FAA safety employees, said the issue was isolated to two ⁠routers that were updated Friday. An official told Reuters it was believed the routers were in Arkansas and Texas. An FAA official said the agency conducted a safety assessment before the work. The union said PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop. L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and is supporting the FAA in its investigation. Its shares last traded down about 4% after hours on ​Friday. OVERLOADED ​COMMUNICATIONS CENTERS Duffy said the trouble began on Friday afternoon, when air traffic control centers experienced instability in radar ​and communications systems. The router issue led to data overloading other communications centers, ‌officials said. "We had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was (it) gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar," Duffy added. The issue affected communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centers, which control aircraft during the cruise portion of a flight. Bedford said the FAA ordered the ground stop in case a center lost all communications. "No facilities went dark. Nothing was fully lost," Bedford added. The FAA said it was doing additional testing with L3Harris to see if there are any additional risks. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines all canceled about 25% of their flights on Saturday, while JetBlue canceled nearly 45%. Airlines have issued travel waivers allowing passengers to rebook flights for later dates ‌without cost. Though the FAA lifted the ground stop on Friday evening, the disruption for passengers was far from over, with ​tens of thousands of people stranded in airports. Airlines were trying to get flight crews and other personnel in ​position to resume flights. The disruption stranded some college football teams on Friday before games ​scheduled for Saturday. FUNDS SOUGHT TO FIX SYSTEM STRAIN Friday's disruption is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset ‌by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several ​thousand controllers. Duffy called on Friday for $50 billion in funding ​to upgrade air traffic control systems, up from his earlier request of $30 billion — after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. item.title: SpaceX catches Starship at launch pad 22 hours after liftoff in a dramatic first
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier. It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel. Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad. The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower. “Can you believe it?” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!” Calling it an “epic day,” Musk later ascended the launch tower to take up-close video with his phone. He even hugged the spacecraft. “Looks great,” he reported via X. SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique. NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars. “It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. “Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag)." The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites. Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps. It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit. SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well. As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause. SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice. Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface.
